title: Data Structures and Algorithms Reference
description: A short reminder of each DSA idea, when it helps, and how its work grows. Open the linked lesson to see the full example in six languages.

entries.name: Data structures and algorithms
entries.summary: A data structure holds items. An algorithm gives clear steps that work on those items.
notes: Trace a tiny input by hand before writing a larger program.
Choose one language; the DSA ideas carry across languages.

entries.name: Choose a language and run code
entries.summary: Choose one language and copy one complete tab. Browser execution is available for JavaScript; the other examples use local tools.
notes: Target C11, C++17, Python 3, Java 17+, or .NET 8+ as appropriate.
Recompile C, C++, and Java after editing the source file.

entries.name: Counting work and Big O
entries.summary: Big O describes a bound on growth as input size increases, not an exact running time.
notes: Name what work you count and whether you mean worst case.
A single scan is O(n) time and can use O(1) extra space.

entries.name: Array positions
entries.summary: An index names an array position. Valid indexes run from 0 to length minus 1.
notes: Check 0 <= index and index < length before access.
Known-position access is O(1); shifting items can take O(n).

entries.name: Linked lists
entries.summary: A singly linked list stores a value and a next link in each node. The head marks the first node.
notes: An empty next link ends the list.
Walking n nodes takes O(n); changing known links can take O(1).

entries.name: Stacks
entries.summary: A stack follows last in, first out. Push adds at the top; pop removes; peek only reads.
notes: Check for an empty stack before pop or peek.
A fixed-size array stack must also check that room remains.

entries.name: Queues
entries.summary: A queue follows first in, first out. Add at the back and remove from the front.
notes: Check for emptiness before reading or removing.
A circular array queue reuses space left by removed items.

entries.name: Sets and unique items
entries.summary: A set stores distinct items and answers membership questions. Adding a duplicate does not grow it.
notes: Do not rely on a shared iteration order across languages.
Lookup cost depends on whether the set uses scans, trees, or hashing.

entries.name: Maps: keys and values
entries.summary: A map links each unique key to one value. Updating an existing key replaces its value.
notes: Check whether a key exists before assuming a returned value means missing.
An array of pairs is a linear map, not automatically a hash table.

entries.name: Hash tables and collisions
entries.summary: A hash table maps keys to starting slots and uses a collision rule when different keys clash.
notes: Compare full keys, not just hash results.
Bound probing and handle full tables; deletion needs its own rule.

entries.name: Linear Search
entries.summary: Check items in order and stop at the first match. Return -1 if no match exists.
notes: Works on unsorted lists.
Worst time O(n); extra space O(1).

entries.name: Binary Search
entries.summary: Search an ascending list by checking its middle and discarding an unhelpful half.
notes: Input must be sorted; duplicates may return any matching position.
Worst search time O(log n); extra space O(1).

entries.name: Sorting Numbers
entries.summary: Arrange values in ascending or descending order using a chosen comparison rule.
notes: JavaScript numeric sorting needs a comparison such as (a, b) => a - b.
Library calls may mutate the collection; time and space promises differ.

entries.name: Bubble Sort
entries.summary: Repeatedly compare neighbours and swap them when the left value is larger.
notes: This early-stop version has O(n) best and O(n²) worst time.
Extra space O(1); stable because equal neighbours are not swapped.

entries.name: Selection Sort
entries.summary: Find the smallest remaining item and swap it into the next position.
notes: Best and worst time O(n²); extra space O(1).
Long swaps mean this version is not stable.

entries.name: Insertion Sort
entries.summary: Grow a sorted left part by shifting larger items and inserting the next value.
notes: Best time O(n), worst time O(n²), extra space O(1).
Strictly larger comparisons keep this version stable.

entries.name: Recursion
entries.summary: Let a function solve a smaller version of its own problem, with a reachable stop rule.
notes: A base case must stop; each recursive step must make progress.
The shown sum uses O(n) time and O(n) call-stack space.

entries.name: Merge Sort
entries.summary: Recursively sort two halves, then merge their front values into a shared buffer.
notes: Best and worst time O(n log n); extra space O(n).
The left-first tie rule makes this implementation stable.

entries.name: Quick Sort
entries.summary: Partition around a pivot, then recursively sort the parts that exclude the finished pivot.
notes: Average O(n log n), worst O(n²) with this last-item pivot.
Stack space averages O(log n) but can reach O(n); not stable.

entries.name: Two Pointers
entries.summary: Move two position markers inward to find a target-sum pair in a sorted list.
notes: This pair-sum rule requires ascending input and two distinct positions.
Scan time O(n), extra space O(1), excluding sorting.

entries.name: Trees: parents and children
entries.summary: A rooted tree has one root and parent-child branches. A binary tree allows at most two children per node.
notes: A leaf has no children; an empty branch is not a node.
A full traversal is O(n); recursive extra space depends on height.

entries.name: Binary search trees
entries.summary: A BST keeps smaller values in the left branch and larger values in the right branch under a chosen duplicate rule.
notes: Search time follows height: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed.
An empty link means the chosen search path has no match.

entries.name: Heaps and the smallest item
entries.summary: A min-heap is a complete binary tree with each parent no larger than its children. Its root is a minimum.
notes: Array children of index i are 2*i+1 and 2*i+2; check each bound.
Peek is O(1); removal sifts down in O(log n).

entries.name: Tree Traversal
entries.summary: Visit a binary tree in inorder by visiting left, recording the node, then visiting right.
notes: O(n) time; O(h) call stack for height h, plus any saved output.
Sorted output requires a binary search tree, not just any binary tree.

entries.name: Graphs and neighbours
entries.summary: A graph has vertices and edges. Neighbours share a direct edge; reachable vertices may need several edges.
notes: An undirected adjacency matrix is symmetric across its diagonal.
Matrix space is O(V²); adjacency-list space is O(V + E).

entries.name: Breadth-First Search
entries.summary: Use a queue to explore graph nodes in layers, marking each node when it is queued.
notes: Adjacency-list time O(V + E), extra space O(V).
One start covers its reachable group; shortest-link layers assume unweighted links.

entries.name: Depth-First Search
entries.summary: Explore one unvisited neighbour deeply, then return to try remaining neighbours.
notes: Mark before following links; adjacency-list time O(V + E).
Extra space O(V); DFS does not promise a shortest path.

entries.name: Dynamic Programming
entries.summary: Save answers to repeated smaller problems and build later answers from them.
notes: The stair-count table uses O(n) time and O(n) space.
Base case: one empty plan reaches zero stairs; only one- or two-stair moves allowed.
